hero.title: Truth or dare for couples, with nothing to set up
hero.description: 70 cards, one phone sitting between the two of you, and you're the one who calls truth or dare.

section1.title: A truth or dare you play, not a list you scroll
section1.p1: Truth or dare for couples, everyone has played it at least once. At camp, at a party, on a sofa at two in the morning… The trouble is what you find online these days: a hundred questions in a row that you scroll through with your thumb. It holds up for five minutes. Then someone reads ahead, someone else hunts for “a better one”, and the game dies.
section1.p2: This one is an actual game. Whoever's turn it is calls their side, a card lands, and you only ever see one at a time. No list, no order you already know, no way to spot what's coming. And cards don't come back around until the deck runs dry.
section1.p3: One phone between the two of you, and off you go!

section2.title: The rules, in four points
section2.intro: They are very short… which is rather the point of the game.
section2.regle1Texte: The game announces whose turn it is on every card. No more counting in your head, no more bickering over who went last.
section2.regle2Texte: Each turn, the named player calls their side. The type is yours to choose. The content of the card isn't: it's drawn at random from the matching deck, and you discover it at the same time as your partner.
section2.regle3Titre: You do it, or you pass
section2.regle3Texte: Happy with the card? You take it on and the turn passes. Not feeling it? You skip, and a forfeit lands instead. Nobody ever has to explain themselves.
section2.regle4Texte: The button to end the game is always there. At the end, the recap counts the cards you took on and the forfeits you picked up, and you can share it.

section3.title: The rule that changes everything: the right to skip
section3.p1: A truth or dare for two goes wrong the day one of you feels cornered. The forfeit exists for exactly that: it makes skipping normal, expected, unremarkable. Instead of an awkward silence you have to justify, it's simply one more card.
section3.p2: Agree on it before you start: either of you can skip without giving a reason, as often as you like. It sounds backwards, and yet it's what will take you the furthest. Because nobody is playing defensively.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.a1: 70 in total: 30 truths, 24 dares and 16 forfeits, gathered in a single deck. They don't come back around until the deck runs dry, so there's plenty to fill an evening.
faq.q2: Do I need to sign up or install anything?
faq.a2: Neither one! The game runs in your browser, on a phone or a computer. Open the page, type your first names, and the first card lands.
faq.a3: It's built for two, with turns announced on every card. Nothing stops you passing the phone round a bigger group, but the cards are written for a couple.
faq.a4: Yes, on a separate page with its own noticeably more direct deck. That's the naughty version, made for the nights when it's really just the two of you.
faq.a5: Yes, and it works better than you'd think. One of you opens the game, reads the card out loud on video and confirms for both. Truths land perfectly, dares take a bit of imagination…

section4.title: Why this game still works, after all these years
section4.p1: Truth or dare survives generation after generation for a very simple reason: it gives you permission to ask a question you'd never have asked on your own. It isn't you asking, it's the card. And that tiny bit of distance changes absolutely everything.
section4.p2: As a couple, it's often the only way to open certain subjects without turning them into a solemn conversation. Nobody wants to hear “we need to talk”… but everyone will draw a card. It is the same principle as our questions to ask each other, in a lighter form. And on the night you would rather both answer the same question than draw cards, there is a game for counting what each of you has already dared to do.
